For each candidate, it counts matching ThemeRules (rules whose part field equals the name and whose chain matches the node). If the count is non-zero, it's printed.

This is a coverage check, not a full dump. It tells you which parts have styles, but not what those styles are. For the full rules, use dumpStyle (which lists all matching rules, including ::part rules) or dumpTheme.

Note: the candidate list is hardcoded. If you write a custom widget with a part name not in the list, dumpParts won't report it. The list is intentionally small to keep the output readable.

docs.title: 2.5 Output target
docs.text:
All four functions take a std::ostream& defaulting to std::cerr. To dump to a file:

std::ofstream log("dump.txt");
Debug::dumpTree(*root, log);
Debug::dumpTheme(log);

To dump to stdout:

Debug::dumpStyle(*node, std::cout);

The functions don't flush. If you're writing to a file, flush or close the stream before reading it.

docs.title: 2.6 Performance
docs.text:
dumpStyle and dumpTree are cheap — they iterate a node's rules and children. dumpTheme is O(rules). All are synchronous and blocking.

Calling them every frame produces a lot of output. They're meant for one-shot debugging, not continuous logging. For per-frame diagnostics, use Logger instead.

docs.title: 3. Logger
docs.text: Logger is the framework's structured logging system. It's always compiled in (unlike Debug), and it's used by the framework itself to report warnings (unknown properties, invalid values, misuse of APIs).

docs.title: 3.1 The message
docs.text:
struct LogMessage {
    LogLevel    level;
    std::string category;   // "StyleParser", "Layout", "Animations", ...
    std::string file;       // source file (e.g. "assets/game.zstyle")
    int         line;       // 0 if not available
    int         column;     // 0 if not available
    std::string text;
};

enum class LogLevel { Debug, Info, Warning, Error };

Five fields, all optional except level and text. The file / line / column are populated when the logging call site knows its source location (e.g. the style parser, which has parsed a .zstyle file and knows the current line).

docs.title: 3.2 The interface
docs.text:
class ILogger {
public:
    virtual ~ILogger() = default;
    virtual void log(const LogMessage& msg) = 0;
};

One method. Implementations are free to do anything with the message.

docs.title: 3.3 The default logger
docs.text:
ConsoleLogger writes to stderr:

[WARN ] [StyleParser] assets/game.zstyle(45:10): unknown property 'foo'. Ignored.
[ERROR] [StyleParser] assets/game.zstyle: impossibile aprire il file

Format: [LEVEL] [category] file(line:col): text.

If file is empty, the file part is omitted. If line == 0, only the file name is shown (no line/column). If both are empty, only the level and category.

The level is padded to 5 characters for alignment (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR).

docs.title: 3.4 Installing a custom logger
docs.text:
Logger::set(&myLogger);

Logger::set takes an ILogger*. Passing nullptr restores the default ConsoleLogger. The user is responsible for the lifetime of a custom logger — Logger doesn't own it.

A custom logger might:

  • Filter by category or level.
  • Route to std::cout for info, std::cerr for warnings.
  • Collect messages into a buffer for later display.
  • Forward to a game engine's logging system.
  • Write to a file.

Example: a logger that writes only errors to a file:

class FileErrorLogger : public ILogger {
public:
    FileErrorLogger(const char* path) : file(path) {}
    void log(const LogMessage& msg) override {
        if (msg.level != LogLevel::Error &&
            msg.level != LogLevel::Warning) return;
        file << "[" << (int)msg.level << "] "
             << msg.category << ": " << msg.text << "\n";
    }
private:
    std::ofstream file;
};

docs.title: 3.5 Free functions
docs.text:
Five free functions in namespace ZenitUI:

inline void logDebug(const std::string& c, const std::string& f, int l, int col, const std::string& t);
inline void logInfo (const std::string& c, const std::string& f, int l, int col, const std::string& t);
inline void logWarn (const std::string& c, const std::string& f, int l, int col, const std::string& t);
inline void logError(const std::string& c, const std::string& f, int l, int col, const std::string& t);

Each constructs a LogMessage and forwards to Logger::get().log(msg).

Parameters:

  • c: category (a short string like "StyleParser").
  • f: file (source file or asset path). Empty if not applicable.
  • l: line. 0 if not applicable.
  • col: column. 0 if not applicable.
  • t: text.

Typical call sites:

// In the style parser, with full location
logWarn("StyleParser", loc.file, loc.line, loc.col,
        "unknown property '" + k + "'. Ignored.");

// In Layout::addChild, without location
logWarn("Layout", "", 0, 0,
        "addChild called on a node not managed by shared_ptr. "
        "Use X::create() and put this logic in onBuild().");

docs.title: 3.6 Categories used in the framework
docs.text:
Category Where Typical messages StyleParser StyleParser.hpp, StyleAttr.hpp Unknown properties, invalid values, missing transition shorthand, keyframe auto-fills, unreadable files. Layout Layout.hpp addChild misuse (constructor call), missing shared_ptr.

There's no strict registry of categories. New code can use any string. The convention is PascalCase, one or two words, describing the subsystem.

docs.title: 3.7 What gets logged
docs.text:
The framework logs in these situations:

  • Unknown property in .zstyle: StyleParser warns, continues.
  • Invalid value in .zstyle: StyleParser warns, ignores the property.
  • transition-delay without transition: warning, ignored.
  • animation-delay without animation: warning, ignored.
  • Keyframe auto-fill: warning per filled property per keyframe.
  • File not found: error, parse aborted.
  • addChild on a make_shared node: warning, call ignored.

The framework doesn't log on:

  • Missing assets (font, texture, effect) — silent fallback.
  • Unknown selector states (:foo) — silently ignored.
  • Missing filter shaders — silent fallback to unfiltered.
  • Style resolution errors that are recoverable — silent.

The philosophy: log things the user probably didn't intend, but stay silent about fallbacks that are legitimate. A missing font is often fine (the default is used); a typo'd property is usually a bug.

docs.title: 3.8 Logging from user code
docs.text:
There's no requirement to use Logger in user code. It's available if you want:

logInfo("MyGame", "", 0, 0, "player spawned");

But std::printf is simpler for most cases. Logger is most useful when you want the message to go through the same sink as the framework's messages (e.g. a game console overlay).

docs.title: 3.9 Performance
docs.text:
logImpl constructs a LogMessage (a struct with four strings), then calls the logger. The strings are copied. For a call that doesn't actually log (e.g. debug level filtered out by a custom logger), the copy is wasted.

There's no "level check before formatting" optimization. If you log in a hot path, check the level first or use a custom logger that doesn't copy.

In practice, the framework doesn't log in hot paths. The typical warning (unknown property) fires once at parse time. There's no per-frame logging.

docs.title: 4. Test infrastructure
docs.text: tests/Mocks.hpp provides a complete headless test fixture. You can drive the framework through a full frame loop without opening a window, and assert on observable behavior (callbacks fired, states set, rects computed).

docs.title: 4.1 MockRenderer
docs.text:
Implements IRenderer with counting and minimal state:

class MockRenderer : public IRenderer {
public:
    int fillRectCount{0};
    int drawTextCount{0};
    int pushClipCount{0};
    int popClipCount{0};

    float charWidth{8.0f};  // deterministic text measurement

    std::vector<Rect> clipStack;
    Rect currentClip{0, 0, 1e9f, 1e9f};

    // ... method implementations ...

    bool supports(Feature) const override { return false; }
};

Key features:

  • Counting: fillRectCount, drawTextCount, pushClipCount, popClipCount increment on the corresponding calls. Useful for asserting "this node was drawn" or "text was measured".
  • Deterministic text: measureText returns charWidth * length for the width and size for the height. So a 10-char string at font size 20 measures 80 x 20. No font required.
  • Clip stack tracking: the renderer maintains a clipStack and the intersected currentClip. pushClip intersects, popClip restores. This lets tests verify that clipping works without a real GPU.
  • No effects: supports(Feature::Effects) returns false, so filters are skipped in tests unless explicitly enabled.

The mock doesn't actually draw pixels. It just records that draw calls were made. Tests that need to verify visual output would need a real backend with framebuffer readback.

docs.title: 4.2 MockPlatform
docs.text:
Implements IPlatform with scriptable input:

class MockPlatform : public IPlatform {
public:
    Vec2 viewport{800.0f, 600.0f};
    double currentTime{0.0};
    bool shiftDown{false};

    PointerState nextPointer;
    InputEvents nextEvents;

    // ... scripted helpers ...
    void moveMouse(Vec2 pos);
    void pressLeft(Vec2 pos);
    void releaseLeft(Vec2 pos);
    void holdLeft(Vec2 pos);
    void pressRight(Vec2 pos);
    void releaseRight(Vec2 pos);
    void pressKey(int key);
    void typeChar(int c);
};

The pointer state is set via helper methods, then read by the framework on the next beginFrame. The mock clears pressed / released after each read, so edge events only fire once.

Helper semantics:

  • pressLeft(pos) — sets down = true, pressed = true, released = false. The next frame sees a press.
  • holdLeft(pos) — down = true, pressed = false, released = false. Subsequent frames of a held button.
  • releaseLeft(pos) — down = false, pressed = false, released = true.
  • moveMouse(pos) — no buttons, no edges.

So a click sequence is:

platform.pressLeft({50, 50});
env.frame(root);       // framework sees press
platform.releaseLeft({50, 50});
env.frame(root);       // framework sees release

Or, more concisely, using the click helper (see §4.4).

docs.title: 4.3 MockAssetProvider
docs.text:
Implements IAssetProvider returning empty handles for everything:

class MockAssetProvider : public IAssetProvider {
public:
    FontHandle    getFont(std::string_view) override { return {}; }
    TextureHandle getTexture(std::string_view) override { return {}; }
    EffectHandle  getEffect(std::string_view) override { return {}; }
};

This means no fonts, textures, or effects are loaded. The framework falls back to defaults:

  • Text uses the default font (which in the mock renderer has deterministic measurement via charWidth).
  • Background textures are missing (nothing drawn).
  • Effects are unsupported (the mock renderer returns false for supports(Effects)).

For tests that need a specific asset, you'd extend the provider.

docs.title: 4.4 The Env fixture
docs.text:
struct Env {
    MockRenderer      renderer;
    MockPlatform      platform;
    MockAssetProvider assets;

    Env();       // installs the mocks in UIContext, calls reset()
    ~Env();      // nulls the UIContext pointers

    void reset();   // clears Theme, UIContext state, mock counters
    void frame(std::shared_ptr<Layout> root, float dt = 1.0f / 60.0f);
    void click(std::shared_ptr<Layout> root, Vec2 pos);
};

Construction installs the three mocks in UIContext and calls reset(). Destruction nulls the pointers (so subsequent tests don't use dangling references).

reset() clears:

  • Theme (rules, keyframes, root).
  • UIContext focus, capture, targets, flags, portals.
  • MockPlatform state (viewport, time, pointer, events).
  • MockRenderer counters and clip state.
  • Metrics::viewport to {1920, 1080} (a sensible default for tests).

frame(root, dt) runs a single frame:

void frame(std::shared_ptr<Layout> root, float dt = 1.0f / 60.0f) {
    auto& ctx = UIContext::get();
    ctx.beginFrame(dt);
    root->updateTree(dt);
    root->measure(platform.viewport.x, platform.viewport.y);
    root->arrange({0, 0, platform.viewport.x, platform.viewport.y});
    root->draw();
}

This is the same sequence as runFrame + renderFrame, but inlined without the renderer's beginFrame / endFrame (which the mock doesn't need).

click(root, pos) does a full press-and-release sequence:

void click(std::shared_ptr<Layout> root, Vec2 pos) {
    platform.pressLeft(pos);
    frame(root);
    platform.releaseLeft(pos);
    frame(root);
}

Two frames — one for the press, one for the release. Callbacks fire on the appropriate frame.

docs.title: 4.5 Writing a test
docs.text:
The test framework is defined in tests/TestFramework.hpp (not shown, but the API is used throughout the test files). Tests use a simple macro-based syntax:

TEST(SuiteName, test_name) {
    Env env;
    // setup
    // actions
    CHECK(condition);
    CHECK_NEAR(a, b, tolerance);
}

Test files are tests/test_*.cpp. Each file includes TestFramework.hpp and (optionally) Mocks.hpp.

test_main.cpp:

int main() {
    ZenitUI::Metrics::viewport = { 1920.0f, 1080.0f };
    return Test::run();
}

Sets the viewport for tests that use vw / vh before running all registered tests.

docs.title: 4.6 Example: click test
docs.text:
TEST(Interaction_click, simple_click_increments) {
    Env env;
    int count = 0;

    auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));

    auto btn = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    btn->size(Px(100), Px(50));
    btn->setInteractive(true);
    btn->setBlocksRaycast(true);
    btn->onClick = [&count]() { count++; };

    root->addChild(btn);

    env.frame(root);       // layout settles
    env.click(root, {50, 25});

    CHECK(count == 1);
}

Steps:

  1. Create the fixture (installs mocks, resets state).
  2. Build a tree.
  3. Run one frame so layout is computed.
  4. Simulate a click.
  5. Assert the callback fired.

The env.frame(root) before the click is required — without it, the button's rect is {0, 0, 0, 0} (no measure/arrange has run), and the hit-test at (50, 25) won't find it.

docs.title: 4.7 Example: hover test
docs.text:
TEST(Interaction_hover, enter_fires_on_move) {
    Env env;
    int enters = 0;

    auto btn = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    btn->size(Px(100), Px(50));
    btn->setInteractive(true);
    btn->setBlocksRaycast(true);
    btn->onHoverEnter = [&enters]() { enters++; };

    auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));
    root->addChild(btn);

    env.frame(root);
    CHECK(enters == 0);

    env.platform.moveMouse({50, 25});
    env.frame(root);
    CHECK(enters == 1);

    env.platform.moveMouse({500, 500});
    env.frame(root);
    // enters still 1 (no exit handler, so no change in enters)
}

The pattern: moveMouse sets the pointer position, frame runs the frame with that position, and the framework updates the hover flags.

docs.title: 4.8 Example: keyboard test
docs.text:
TEST(Interaction_focus, tab_cycles_through_focusables) {
    Env env;

    auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));

    auto a = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    a->size(Px(100), Px(50));
    a->setInteractive(true);
    a->setBlocksRaycast(true);
    a->setFocusable(true);

    auto b = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    b->size(Px(100), Px(50));
    b->setInteractive(true);
    b->setBlocksRaycast(true);
    b->setFocusable(true);

    root->addChild(a);
    root->addChild(b);

    env.frame(root);

    env.platform.pressKey(Key::Tab);
    env.frame(root);
    CHECK(UIContext::get().hasFocus(a.get()));

    env.platform.pressKey(Key::Tab);
    env.frame(root);
    CHECK(UIContext::get().hasFocus(b.get()));

    env.platform.pressKey(Key::Tab);
    env.frame(root);
    CHECK(UIContext::get().hasFocus(a.get()));   // wrap
}

Each pressKey sets nextEvents.keys, which is consumed by the next pollInputEvents call. So the Tab event is seen on the following frame.

docs.title: 4.9 Example: style test
docs.text:
TEST(Parser_basic, hover_state) {
    Theme t;
    ZMarkup::loadStyleString("Toggle:hover { background: blue; }", t);
    CHECK(t.rules.size() == 1);
    CHECK(t.rules[0].chain.size() == 1);
    CHECK(t.rules[0].chain[0].requireHover);
}

Parser tests don't need Env — they operate on a local Theme. This is faster and simpler for testing the parsing layer.

docs.title: 4.10 What can be tested
docs.text:
• Style parsing: parse a string, check Theme::rules, Style::customProps, etc.
  • Style resolution: build a node, run a frame, check node->getStyle().
  • Layout: build a tree, run measure/arrange, check getRect().
  • Interaction: simulate clicks/keys, check callbacks and state.
  • Animation: run N frames, check that a property interpolated.
  • Media queries: set Metrics::viewport, check that rules match.
  • ZMarkup: build a string, check the tree.

docs.title: 4.11 What can't be tested with the mocks
docs.text:
• Visual output: the mock renderer doesn't draw pixels. Tests can't verify colors, shapes, or text rendering.
  • Text measurement accuracy: the mock uses charWidth * length, which is a rough approximation. Tests that depend on precise text size should use a real backend.
  • Effects: the mock returns false for supports(Effects), so filters and shaders are skipped.
  • Render targets: the mock's createTarget returns an invalid handle, so any code that relies on a valid target won't work.
  • Performance: the mocks are fast, but they don't measure real rendering performance.

For these, you need a real backend. The Raylib backend can be used headlessly (no window) with an offscreen framebuffer, but that's not currently set up.

docs.title: 5.1 "My widget doesn't appear"
docs.text:
1. Debug::dumpTree(*root, std::cout); — is the widget in the tree?
  2. If yes: Debug::dumpStyle(*widget, std::cout); — does it have a non-zero rect? Are the expected rules matched?
  3. If the rect is {0,0,0,0}: check the parent's size and the widget's width / height / intrinsic size.
  4. If the rect is fine but nothing is drawn: check supports(Effects) and the filter chain (a missing shader silently draws nothing for filtered nodes).

docs.title: 5.2 "My styles don't apply"
docs.text:
1. Debug::dumpTheme(std::cout); — is the rule loaded?
  2. Debug::dumpStyle(*node, std::cout); — is the rule matching?
  3. If the rule isn't in matches: check the selector. Specificity? Media query? State flags?
  4. If the rule matches but the value is wrong: check the cascade order. Inline styles beat CSS. Later same-specificity rules beat earlier ones. !important doesn't exist.
  5. Check customProps if using var().

docs.title: 5.3 "My click doesn't fire"
docs.text:
1. Is the node interactive? setInteractive(true).
  2. Does it blocksRaycast? Check the parent chain.
  3. Is there a node on top that's consuming? Use UIContext::get().topmostConsumer after a frame.
  4. Is the press and release on the same node? A drag-out-drag-in might not fire.
  5. Is onClick even set? Check with a breakpoint or a log.

docs.title: 5.4 "My layout is wrong"
docs.text:
1. Debug::dumpTree(*root, std::cout); — check the rects.
  2. Is the parent the right size? Check recursively.
  3. Is the child's intrinsic size what you expect? computeIntrinsicSize might be returning 0.
  4. Is grow / shrink distributing space correctly? Check the container's main-axis size vs. the sum of children.
  5. Is justify / items-* doing what you expect? Check the align values.

docs.title: 5.5 "My animation doesn't run"
docs.text:
1. Is the animation / transition property parsed? Check dumpStyle output.
  2. Is the keyframe name defined? Check dumpTheme.
  3. Is the state correct? :hover needs isHovered, :checked needs setChecked(true).
  4. Is the animation ticked? tickCss runs every frame in update.
  5. For imperative: is addAnimation + playAnimation called? Is the name correct?

docs.title: 5.6 "My filter doesn't work"
docs.text:
1. Is the shader loaded? assets.loadEffect(name, path).
  2. Is the filter registered? FilterRegistry::get().add(def).
  3. Is the name in .zstyle matching? Check dumpStyle.
  4. Is the backend supporting effects? supports(Feature::Effects).
  5. Is the node inside another target? renderer->inTarget().

docs.title: 6.1 Custom logger for tests
docs.text:
Tests can install a logger that fails on any error:

class FailingLogger : public ILogger {
public:
    void log(const LogMessage& msg) override {
        if (msg.level == LogLevel::Error) {
            std::cerr << "UNEXPECTED ERROR: " << msg.text << "\n";
            std::abort();
        }
    }
};

This makes tests fail on unexpected errors, catching silent bugs.

docs.title: 6.2 Custom logger for production
docs.text:
A production logger might:

  • Write to a rolling file.
  • Forward errors to a crash reporter.
  • Filter out Debug messages.
  • Prefix messages with a timestamp.

The Logger::set(&custom) call is the only integration point.

docs.title: 6.3 Logging in a game loop
docs.text:
If you log every frame, the console fills up. Filter aggressively:

class FrameLogger : public ILogger {
public:
    void log(const LogMessage& msg) override {
        if (msg.level == LogLevel::Error)
            console.Print(msg.text);
        // drop warnings in release
    }
};

Or accumulate and show only on a keypress (a "debug overlay").

docs.title: 7.1 Dumping the tree on a key press
docs.text:
if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_F1)) {
    Debug::dumpTree(*root, std::cout);
}
if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_F2)) {
    Debug::dumpTheme(std::cout);
}

Requires ZENITUI_DEBUG to be defined. In a release build, the calls are no-ops (the stubs compile to nothing).

docs.title: 7.2 Highlighting a specific node
docs.text:
There's no built-in "highlight" in the renderer. To visually debug a node's position, add a debug border:

node->getInlineBase().borderColor = Colors::Red;
node->getInlineBase().borderWidth = Px(1);

Or, temporarily, add a child that draws a red rect. A future extension might add a debug overlay.

docs.title: 7.3 Tracing style resolution
docs.text:
Add a breakpoint in StyleResolver::resolveFor, or log inside:

logDebug("Style", "", 0, 0,
    "resolving " + node.getStyleTag() + " with " +
    std::to_string(matches.size()) + " matches");

This requires temporarily modifying the framework source. A less invasive approach: dump the theme once at startup and inspect the rules manually.

docs.title: 7.4 Tracing input
docs.text:
Log in InputController::fireCallbacks:

if (node.onClick) {
    logDebug("Input", "", 0, 0, "click on " + node.getStyleTag());
}

Again, requires modifying the source.

docs.title: 7.5 Inspecting UIContext
docs.text:
UIContext::get() is a singleton. You can inspect it from anywhere:

auto& ctx = UIContext::get();
std::cout << "pointer: " << ctx.pointer.pos.x << "," << ctx.pointer.pos.y << "\n";
std::cout << "topmost: " << (ctx.topmostConsumer ? ctx.topmostConsumer->getStyleTag() : "none") << "\n";
std::cout << "focused: " << (ctx.focusedNode.lock() ? "yes" : "no") << "\n";

Useful for understanding why a click isn't reaching a node.

docs.title: 8. Pitfalls
docs.text:
ZENITUI_DEBUG must be defined before including Debug.hpp.

Defining it after the include has no effect. The stub branch is already active. To enable debug functions in a specific file:

#define ZENITUI_DEBUG
#include "Debug.hpp"

Or use the compiler flag: -DZENITUI_DEBUG.

dumpTree prints the logical tree, not the visual tree.

Portals appear where they're declared, not where they're drawn. Absolute-positioned nodes appear in their parent's children list, not at their screen position. The rects are correct, but the tree structure doesn't reflect z-order or portal destinations.

dumpStyle only shows ::part rules that match the node.

The matches list includes ::part rules (since they match the node with a state), but dumpStyle doesn't distinguish them from regular rules. Look for the ::part suffix in the selector string.

dumpParts uses a hardcoded candidate list.

If your widget defines a part not in the list ("track", "fill", "knob", "box", "mark", "cursor"), dumpParts won't report it. Use dumpStyle instead, or extend the list.

The Logger doesn't filter by level.

The default ConsoleLogger prints everything. If you want to filter, install a custom logger. There's no built-in level setting.

Missing assets are silent.

resolveFont, resolveBgTexture, resolveEffectIfNeeded, and FilterRegistry::applyFilter all fall back silently when the name isn't found. This is intentional (the framework works without assets), but it means a typo'd font name produces no error — just the default font.

The mock renderer's measureText is a rough approximation.

charWidth * length doesn't account for kerning, variable-width fonts, or even spaces (a space has the same width as a letter in the mock). Tests that rely on precise text measurement should use a real backend.

env.frame doesn't call renderFrame's beginFrame / endFrame.

The mock renderer's beginFrame / endFrame are no-ops, so it doesn't matter. If you extend the mock to do per-frame setup, you'd need to add those calls.

The Env destructor nulls the UIContext pointers.

If a test creates an Env inside a scope and then uses a Layout from that scope after it, the Layout's destructor might try to use the renderer (via ~Layout's destroyTarget). With the pointer nulled, this is safe — the destructor checks for null.

But if the Env is alive and the Layout is destroyed after the Env, the Layout uses the (still valid) mock renderer. If the Env was destroyed, the pointer is null and the check saves it.

Tests don't reset Theme automatically.

Env::reset() clears Theme::get(), but a test that creates an Env outside a loop and reuses it across test cases should call env.reset() between cases. Most tests create a fresh Env per case (the fixture is cheap), so this isn't an issue.

dumpTheme can be very large.

A stylesheet with hundreds of rules produces hundreds of lines of output. Redirect to a file or filter with a custom logger.

Debug functions don't flush.

std::cerr is unbuffered (or line-buffered) by default. std::cout is buffered. If you're writing to a file, flush explicitly.

The Debug stubs take the same parameters.

The no-op stubs in the #else branch have the same signatures, so calls compile in both modes. This is intentional — you can leave debug calls in the code without conditionals.

But the stubs don't evaluate their arguments. So Debug::dumpTree(*node) compiles to nothing — node isn't dereferenced. If node were a nullptr, the release build wouldn't crash (the stub ignores it), but the debug build would. A subtle difference, but usually irrelevant.

Logger is a singleton.

Logger::get() returns a static instance. Logger::set(&custom) replaces the current logger. This is process-wide — all tests, all subsystems share the same logger.

If you install a custom logger in one test and forget to restore it, subsequent tests use it. Use Logger::set(nullptr) to restore the default, or scope the custom logger with an RAII wrapper.

The mock's text measurement uses the string's length, not its size.

measureText does charWidth * (float)s.size(). For ASCII, this is the character count. For multi-byte UTF-8, this is the byte count, which overestimates. Since the framework only handles ASCII currently, this isn't an issue in practice.

The Env fixture doesn't set Metrics::viewport to the platform's viewport.

Env::reset() sets Metrics::viewport = {1920, 1080} (a default) and platform.viewport = {800, 600}. The first beginFrame overwrites Metrics::viewport with platform.viewport. So before the first frame, Metrics::viewport is {1920, 1080}, and after it's {800, 600}. If a test reads Metrics::viewport before calling frame, it gets the wrong value.

The reason for the discrepancy: Metrics::viewport is a global, and some tests (e.g. test_value_parsers.cpp) read it before setting up a mock. The default {1920, 1080} is a sensible choice for those tests. Once Env runs a frame, the platform's viewport takes over.

Tests share global state.

Theme, UIContext, Metrics are all singletons. Tests that modify them affect subsequent tests unless reset. Env::reset() handles the common cases (Theme::clear(), UIContext fields), but a test that sets Metrics::viewport without an Env leaves it modified.

In practice, test_main.cpp sets Metrics::viewport = {1920, 1080} at the start, and tests that need a specific viewport set it explicitly. The framework doesn't restore between tests, so ordering matters. Keep this in mind when a test passes alone but fails in a suite.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This guide walks you through the minimum viable setup: initialize a backend, create a root layout, add a widget, and run the frame loop.

By the end you will have a window with a styled, clickable button.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C++20 or newer.
  • A backend. ZenitUI ships a reference implementation for Raylib, but the core only depends on three abstract interfaces declared in UIContext.hpp:
Interface Responsibility IRenderer Primitive drawing, text measurement, clip / transform / target IPlatform Window, pointer, keyboard, timers, DPI, safe area IAssetProvider Fonts, textures, shaders, keyed by string name

If you want to use a different graphics library, implement those three and you're done. Nothing else in the framework touches the GPU.

docs.title: 2. Initialize the backend
docs.text:
ZenitUI is a library, not a framework that owns main(). You initialize the backend, hand it to UIContext, and drive the frame loop yourself.

#include <raylib.h>
#include "RaylibBackend.hpp"
#include "UI.hpp"

using namespace ZenitUI;

int main() {
    InitWindow(800, 600, "ZenitUI");
    SetWindowState(FLAG_WINDOW_RESIZABLE);

    // 1. Backend instances
    RaylibRenderer      renderer;
    RaylibPlatform      platform;
    RaylibAssetProvider assets(renderer);

    // 2. Register them on the global context
    UIContext::get().renderer = &renderer;
    UIContext::get().platform = &platform;
    UIContext::get().assets   = &assets;

    // 3. Load any asset you'll reference by name from .zstyle / ZMarkup
    assets.loadFont("calibri", "assets/calibri.ttf", 64);
    assets.loadTexture("bubble", "assets/bubble.png");
    assets.loadEffect("blur",    "assets/blur.fs");

    // ...
}

Rule of thumb: anything you want to reference by name (in a .zstyle file or in a ZMarkup attribute) must be registered with the IAssetProvider before the first frame. Fonts, textures, and shaders are all referenced by string.

UIContext is a singleton. It owns:

  • the three backend pointers,
  • the current input snapshot (pointer, inputEvents, shiftHeld),
  • the focus / pointer-capture / portal registries,
  • the frame clock (dt, time).

You generally don't touch it directly after setup, except for advanced cases (see Events and Portals).

docs.title: 3. Create a root layout
docs.text:
The root is just a Layout that fills the viewport. Everything else is a child of it.

auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));
root->getInlineBase().itemsH = Align::Center;
root->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;

LayoutType::Stack lays out children on top of each other, positioned by itemsH / itemsV. Use LayoutType::Vertical for a column and LayoutType::Horizontal for a row. See Layout for the full list of container properties.

docs.title: Equivalent root in ZMarkup
docs.text:
auto ui = ZMarkup::build(R"(
    Stack#root {
        // children go here
    }
)");
auto root = ui.root();

Then put the sizing / alignment into a .zstyle file:

#root {
    width: 100%;
    height: 100%;
    items-h: center;
    items-v: center;
}

Both approaches are equivalent. Choose whichever is more comfortable — you can mix them freely in the same project.

docs.title: 4. Add a widget
docs.text:
Widgets live in namespace ZenitUI::UI and are created via their ::create() factory (or a helper like Btn / Label).

auto btn = Btn("Click me", []{
    std::printf("clicked!\n");
});
btn->cls("btn-primary");

root->addChild(btn);

Btn(text, callback) is a small helper that creates a Button and adds a Text child with class "btn-text". If you want full control, use Button::create(cb) directly and add whatever child you want.

Every widget is a Layout subclass, so it inherits:

  • .cls("name") / .id("name") / .size(w, h) fluent helpers,
  • getInlineBase() for inline style overrides,
  • addChild() / removeFromParent(),
  • callback fields onClick, onPress, onRelease, onHoverEnter, onHoverExit, onRightClick.

docs.title: The same widget in ZMarkup
docs.text:
auto ui = ZMarkup::build(R"(
    Stack#root {
        Button.btn-primary#go "Click me"
    }
)");
ui.onClick("go", []{ std::printf("clicked!\n"); });

You can also bind to #root if you want the click to fire when clicking outside the button — see Events for bubbling rules.

docs.title: Styling the button
docs.text:
Without .zstyle, the button will use only the widget's built-in defaults. To actually make it look like something, load a stylesheet:

ZMarkup::loadStyleFile("assets/game.zstyle");

/* assets/game.zstyle */
.btn-primary {
    background: #0079F1;
    radius: 8px;
    padding: 1.5vh 2vw;
    min-width: 80px;
    transition: background 0.25s ease-out-quad, scale 0.12s ease-out-back;
}
.btn-primary:hover   { background: #3296FF; scale: 1.15; }
.btn-primary:pressed { background: #505050; scale: 0.90; }

loadStyleFile appends rules to the global Theme. Calling it multiple times is fine — rules accumulate, and later rules with the same specificity win. See ZStyle for the full language.

docs.title: 5. Run the frame loop
docs.text:
Each frame has two phases: a logic phase and a draw phase.

while (!WindowShouldClose()) {
    float dt = GetFrameTime();

    // ---- logic phase (no GL calls inside) ----
    root->runFrame(dt);

    // ---- draw phase ----
    BeginDrawing();
    ClearBackground(BLACK);
    root->renderFrame();
    EndDrawing();
}

runFrame(dt) expands to:

UIContext::get().beginFrame(dt);   // poll platform, refresh input, advance clock
root->updateTree(dt);              // state FSM, style resolve, animations, focus
root->measure(viewport.x, viewport.y);   // bottom-up intrinsic size
root->arrange({0, 0, viewport.x, viewport.y}); // top-down positioning

renderFrame() expands to:

renderer->beginFrame();   // e.g. push DPI scale matrix
root->draw();
renderer->endFrame();

Why the split? Because measure / arrange don't touch the GPU, and draw doesn't touch input. Keeping them apart makes headless tests trivial (see Mocks.hpp) and lets you run the logic at a different rate from rendering if you ever need to.

docs.title: 6. The complete program
docs.text:
#include <raylib.h>
#include "RaylibBackend.hpp"
#include "UI.hpp"
#include <cstdio>

using namespace ZenitUI;
using namespace ZenitUI::UI;

int main() {
    InitWindow(800, 600, "ZenitUI");
    SetWindowState(FLAG_WINDOW_RESIZABLE);

    RaylibRenderer      renderer;
    RaylibPlatform      platform;
    RaylibAssetProvider assets(renderer);

    UIContext::get().renderer = &renderer;
    UIContext::get().platform = &platform;
    UIContext::get().assets   = &assets;

    assets.loadFont("calibri", "assets/calibri.ttf", 64);
    ZMarkup::loadStyleFile("assets/game.zstyle");

    auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
    root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));
    root->getInlineBase().itemsH = Align::Center;
    root->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;

    auto btn = Btn("Click me", []{ std::printf("clicked!\n"); });
    btn->cls("btn-primary");
    root->addChild(btn);

    while (!WindowShouldClose()) {
        root->runFrame(GetFrameTime());

        BeginDrawing();
        ClearBackground(GetColor(0x181818FF));
        root->renderFrame();
        EndDrawing();
    }

    CloseWindow();
    return 0;
}

You now have a running ZenitUI app with a styled button that reacts to hover, press, and click — the rules in game.zstyle do the styling, the Btn(...) helper does the rest.

docs.title: 7. Optional: keyboard focus
docs.text:
Add setFocusable(true) to a node if you want it to be reachable by Tab and to react to Enter / Space:

auto btn = Btn("Click me", []{ /* ... */ });
btn->setFocusable(true);
btn->setKeyboardActivates(true);   // Enter / Space fire onClick

Then press Tab at runtime — the button gains focus, :focus rules from .zstyle apply, and pressing Enter fires the click callback. See Events for the full focus / navigation model.

docs.title: 8. Next steps
docs.text:
• Layout — grow, shrink, gap, justify, items-*, absolute positioning, units.
  • Widgets — every built-in component with props and events.
  • ZMarkup — build complex trees declaratively.
  • ZStyle — selector syntax, states, ::part, var(), calc(), @media.
  • Events — bubbling, pointer capture, focus, right-click, context menus.
  • Animations — transitions, @keyframes, imperative animations.
  • Portals — Popup, Tooltip, Dropdown, Modal.
  • Effects — filters, shaders, FilterRegistry.
  • Custom Widgets — build your own component.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
"My widget doesn't appear." Check that (a) the parent has a non-zero size, (b) the widget has a non-zero intrinsic size or an explicit width / height, and (c) you called runFrame before renderFrame at least once — the first runFrame is what computes rect.

"My click callback never fires." The node must be interactive and reachable by hit-test. Layout defaults to interactive = true, but custom widgets sometimes set it to false (e.g. Panel, Text). Check setBlocksRaycast too — a node that only blocks raycast won't receive onClick.

"My style rules don't apply." - Selector specificity matters. .card Button beats Button. - Inline styles (getInlineBase()) beat any rule. - State rules (:hover, :checked) only match while the state flag is set on the node — see Events. - :focus requires setFocusable(true). - Media queries (@media) are evaluated against Metrics::viewport, not the OS window size — see ZStyle.

"My text is not wrapping." Set setWrap(true) on the Text (or wrap in ZMarkup). Wrapping also needs an available width — an auto-sized container gives the text an infinite width, so it will never wrap. Give the parent a fixed or percentage width.

"My font name doesn't resolve." Font names in .zstyle (font: calibri;) and ZMarkup (font="calibri") must match a name registered with IAssetProvider::loadFont. Names are case-sensitive.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: ZenitUI has three container types and a Flexbox-inspired property set. If you know CSS Flexbox, most concepts will feel familiar — but the names are simplified and the defaults differ in a few places.

docs.title: 1. Container types
docs.text:
Every Layout has a LayoutType set at construction:

Type Direction Purpose LayoutType::Stack none (overlay) Children are placed on top of each other, aligned by items-h / items-v. LayoutType::Vertical top → bottom Children flow vertically. LayoutType::Horizontal left → right Children flow horizontally. 
auto col = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Vertical);
auto row = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Horizontal);
auto stk = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);

VStack { ... }
HStack { ... }
Stack  { ... }

VStack() / HStack() are helpers that also set the style tag to "VStack" / "HStack", so .zstyle rules like VStack { ... } apply.

docs.title: Which one should I use?
docs.text:
• Stack — anything that is "a box with stuff inside, positioned freely" (Panels, Buttons, Cards, Toggles). Children are typically positioned with align-h / align-v on themselves, or with position: absolute.
  • Vertical — settings lists, sidebars, scrollable content, forms.
  • Horizontal — toolbars, button rows, label-value rows.

docs.title: 2. Units
docs.text: Every size-like property accepts a Value, which is a sum of terms. Each term has a coefficient and a unit. This is what makes calc() work.

docs.title: Supported units
calc()
docs.text:
calc() supports +, -, *, /, parentheses, and mixed units:

width: calc(100% - 20px);
height: calc(50vh + 2 * 12px);
left: calc((100% - 40px) / 2);

The parser builds a Value with multiple terms; resolution happens lazily against the parent's dimensions when the node is measured.

auto v = parseValueToken("calc(100% - 20px)").value();
// v.terms = [ {100, Percent}, {-20, Pixel} ]

docs.title: Inline constructors
docs.text:
btn->size(Px(120), Px(40));
btn->size(Percent(100), Auto());
btn->size(VW(30), VH(6));

Button "OK" width="120px" height="40px"
Button "OK" width="100%" height="auto"

docs.title: 3. Sizing
docs.text: Every node has width, height, min-width, max-width, min-height, max-height. All accept any Value, including auto.

docs.title: auto behavior
docs.text:
• On the root: auto resolves to 0 unless the parent supplies a bounded space, in which case it takes the available space (only for the main axis in Vertical/Horizontal).
  • Inside a container: auto means "use my intrinsic size". For most nodes that's 0×0 unless children or computeIntrinsicSize say otherwise. For Text it's the measured text box; for widgets like Checkbox and ProgressBar there's a default intrinsic size.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
min-* and max-* clamp the final size after all other calculations:

card->getInlineBase().minWidth  = Px(80);
card->getInlineBase().maxWidth  = Percent(60);

.card {
    min-width: 80px;
    max-width: 60vw;
}

If max-width ends up smaller than min-width, max-width wins (matches CSS behavior: the clamp function returns hi when hi < lo).

docs.title: padding
docs.text:
Inside the node, before children are placed.

card->getInlineBase().padding = Spacing(VH(3), VW(2));

.card { padding: 3vh 2vw; }        /* vertical | horizontal */
.card { padding: 8px; }            /* all sides */
.card { padding: 1px 2px 3px 4px; }/* top right bottom left */

docs.title: margin
docs.text:
Outside the node, pushing it away from its siblings.

.card { margin: 0 0 8px 0; }

Margins are respected in Vertical / Horizontal flow and in absolute positioning. In Stack, margins still apply to the node's own rect but children are not pushed around each other.

docs.title: gap
docs.text:
Space between siblings in Vertical / Horizontal. Ignored by Stack.

row->getInlineBase().gap = VW(0.5f);

.row { gap: 8px; }

docs.title: 5. Flex: grow, shrink
docs.text:
When a Vertical / Horizontal container has leftover (or missing) space along its main axis, children with grow / shrink absorb it.

Property Default Meaning grow 0 If there's leftover space, distribute proportionally to grow. shrink 1 If space is negative, shrink proportionally to shrink. 
sidebar->getInlineBase().shrink = 0;   // never shrink
content->getInlineBase().grow   = 1;   // take all leftover space

.spacer-grow { grow: 1; }
.demo-sidebar { shrink: 0; }

Distribution algorithm (per container, main axis only):

  1. Sum the fixed sizes (margin + measured size + margin) of all in-flow children, plus gap × (N-1).
  2. freeSpace = containerInnerSize - totalFixedSize.
  3. If freeSpace > 0 and totalGrow > 0: each child gets freeSpace × (childGrow / totalGrow) added to its size.
  4. If freeSpace < 0 and totalShrink > 0: each child gets freeSpace × (childShrink / totalShrink) added (i.e. removed) from its size.
  5. Final sizes are clamped by min-* / max-*.

Common patterns:

// Two-column layout: left fixed, right fills
auto row = HStack({ sidebar, content });
sidebar->getInlineBase().shrink = 0;
content->getInlineBase().grow   = 1;

// Three columns with 1 : 2 : 1 ratio
a->getInlineBase().grow = 1;
b->getInlineBase().grow = 2;
c->getInlineBase().grow = 1;

docs.title: 6. Alignment
docs.text:
There are two axes and two levels of alignment:

  • justify — main axis of the container (horizontal in Horizontal, vertical in Vertical). Applies to the whole group of children.
  • items-h / items-v — cross axis of the container. Default for children that don't override.
  • align-h / align-v — set on the child, overrides the container's items-* for that specific child.

docs.title: justify (main axis)
docs.text:
Only has an effect when freeSpace > 0 and totalGrow == 0.

Value Behavior Justify::Start Children packed at the start (default). Justify::Center Children centered as a group. Justify::End Children packed at the end. Justify::SpaceBetween First child at start, last at end, space distributed evenly between. 
row->getInlineBase().justify = Justify::SpaceBetween;

.row { justify: space-between; }

docs.title: items-h / items-v (cross axis)
docs.text:
Set on the container, applies to all children:

Value Behavior Align::Start Child at the start of the cross axis (default). Align::Center Child centered on the cross axis. Align::End Child at the end of the cross axis. Align::Stretch Child is stretched to fill the cross axis. Align::Auto Child picks its own (usually means Start). 
root->getInlineBase().itemsH = Align::Center;
root->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;

#root {
    items-h: center;
    items-v: center;
}

docs.title: align-h / align-v (per-child override)
docs.text:
Set on the child itself:

auto label = Label("hi");
label->getInlineBase().alignH = Align::End;   // overrides parent's itemsH

.setting-label { align-h: end; }

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Container justify axis items-h axis items-v axis Horizontal horizontal vertical (unused) Vertical vertical (unused) horizontal Stack (ignored) horizontal vertical

Note: in Horizontal, items-v is the cross-axis alignment; in Vertical, items-h is the cross-axis alignment. items-h / items-v are still both read in Stack because there is no main axis — the container behaves like a Stack of one child per position.

docs.title: Centering anything
docs.text:
// Center a widget in its parent
parent->getInlineBase().itemsH = Align::Center;
parent->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;

.parent {
    items-h: center;
    items-v: center;
}

This works for both Stack (positions the single child) and Vertical / Horizontal (positions all children along the cross axis).

docs.title: 7. Absolute positioning
docs.text:
A node with position: absolute is removed from the flow and positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor's inner box (i.e. inside its padding).

badge->getInlineBase().position = Position::Absolute;
badge->getInlineBase().top      = Px(8);
badge->getInlineBase().right    = Px(8);

.badge {
    position: absolute;
    top: 8px;
    right: 8px;
}

docs.title: Anchoring rules
docs.text:
Set on the node Effect left only Positioned from the parent's left edge. right only Positioned from the parent's right edge. left + right + width: auto The node stretches horizontally between left and right. top only Positioned from the parent's top edge. bottom only Positioned from the parent's bottom edge. top + bottom + height: auto The node stretches vertically.

Any combination works. If neither left nor right is set, the node sits at the start of the parent's inner box (margin-left still applies).

docs.title: Centering with absolute positioning
docs.text:
To center a node whose size is known:

.center {
    position: absolute;
    top: 50%;
    left: 50%;
    width: 100px;
    translate-x: -50%;
    translate-y: -50%;
}

translate-x: -50% is resolved against the node's own width (resolveSelfH), not the parent's. Same for translate-y.

Note: position: relative in ZenitUI currently behaves like static for layout purposes (the node stays in flow). It only affects stacking (see §10). If you need to visually offset a node, use translate-x / translate-y.

docs.title: 8. Overflow
docs.text:
overflow-x and overflow-y control both clipping and scrolling.

Value Clip Scrollable Notes Overflow::Visible no no Default. Overflow::Hidden yes no Children are clipped. Overflow::Scroll yes yes Scrollbar always visible. Overflow::Auto yes yes Scrollbar only when needed. 
panel->getInlineBase().overflowY = Overflow::Scroll;
panel->getInlineBase().overflowX = Overflow::Hidden;

.panel {
    overflow-y: auto;
    overflow-x: hidden;
}

docs.title: Computed value rule
docs.text:
If one axis is Visible and the other is not, the Visible axis is promoted to Auto. This mirrors the CSS computed-value rule and prevents the "visible in one direction, clip in the other" ambiguity that no backend can represent cleanly. The promotion happens in ComputedStyle::from.

.thing { overflow-x: scroll; overflow-y: visible; }
/* computed: overflow-x = scroll, overflow-y = auto */

docs.title: Scrollable containers
docs.text:
When a node has overflow: scroll | auto, the layout engine:

  1. Measures children without the main-axis constraint, so they can be taller (or wider) than the container.
  2. Arranges children in a virtual space that is max(containerSize, contentSize).
  3. Tracks scroll offset in a ScrollController (see Scroll System).
  4. Draws a scrollbar thumb along the relevant axis, and clips the subtree.

Scrolling behavior:

  • Mouse wheel — vertical by default, horizontal when Shift is held.
  • Dragging the scrollbar thumb.
  • Clicking on the scrollbar track jumps to that position.
  • Inertia after a wheel event (exponential decay).

See Events for how scroll interacts with hover and press states (the "hover freeze" behavior: hover is not recomputed while a scroll is in progress).

docs.title: 9. Transform
docs.text:
Every node can be visually transformed without affecting layout:

Property Type Meaning translate-x Value Horizontal offset, resolved against the node's own width. translate-y Value Vertical offset, resolved against the node's own height. scale float Uniform scale factor around the node's center. rotation float Degrees, clockwise, around the node's center. 
card->getInlineBase().scale      = 1.15f;
card->getInlineBase().rotation   = 3.0f;
card->getInlineBase().translateY = Px(-4);

.card {
    scale: 1.05;
    translate-y: -4px;
}

Pivot is always the node's center. Transform is applied during rendering and hit-testing, not during measure / arrange — a translated node keeps its original rect for layout purposes.

Note: scale also interacts with the "layer" render path used by filters — the render target is sized to the transformed bounding box. See Render Pipeline.

docs.title: 10. z-index and stacking contexts
docs.text:
By default, siblings are drawn in declaration order (last = on top). z-index overrides this.

panel->getInlineBase().position = Position::Relative;
panel->getInlineBase().zIndex   = ZIndex(10);

.panel {
    position: relative;
    z-index: 10;
}

docs.title: Stacking context rules
docs.text:
A node becomes a stacking context if:

  • position != static, and
  • z-index != auto.

Inside a stacking context, children are drawn in three groups:

  1. Children with negative z-index (in ascending order).
  2. Children without a stacking context (declaration order).
  3. Children with positive z-index (in ascending order).

Hit-testing uses the same order, reversed — topmost first, so clicking on an overlapping child reaches the visually topmost one.

A node with z-index set but position: static is not a stacking context and participates in the parent's normal flow.

docs.title: 11. Backgrounds and box-shadow (layout-adjacent)
docs.text:
These don't change layout, but they're usually set alongside layout properties, so here's a quick reference:

.card {
    background: #2A2A32;               /* solid color, RGBA or hex */
    background-texture: bubble;        /* a texture registered by name */
    background-texture: npatches 16 16 16 16;  /* nine-slice with insets */
    radius: 8px;                       /* rounded corners */
    border-width: 1px;
    border-color: #3A3A40;
    box-shadow: 4px 4px 8px #00000080; /* x y blur color */
}

card->getInlineBase().background = Color{42, 42, 50, 255};
card->getInlineBase().radius     = Px(8);
card->setBackgroundTexture(assets.getTexture("bubble"));

Draw order inside a node:

  1. box-shadow (behind everything).
  2. background color.
  3. background-texture (stretched or nine-sliced).
  4. border.
  5. renderContent (widget-specific: slider track, checkbox mark, text…).
  6. Children (in z-order).

For the full list of paintable properties, see ZStyle.

docs.title: Full-viewport root
docs.text:
auto root = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
root->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));

#root { width: 100%; height: 100%; }

docs.title: Sidebar + content (two-column)
docs.text:
auto row = HStack({ sidebar, content });
sidebar->size(VW(20), Percent(100));
sidebar->getInlineBase().shrink = 0;
content->getInlineBase().grow   = 1;
content->getInlineBase().height = Percent(100);

.demo-panel  { display: horizontal; gap: 2vw; }
.demo-sidebar{ width: 20vw; height: 100%; shrink: 0; }
.demo-content{ grow: 1; height: 100%; }

docs.title: Button row
docs.text:
auto row = HStack({ Btn("A"), Btn("B"), Btn("C") });
row->getInlineBase().gap = Px(4);
row->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;

.button-row { gap: 4px; items-v: center; }

docs.title: Card with fixed padding
docs.text:
auto card = VStack();
card->getInlineBase().padding = Spacing(VH(3), VW(2));
card->getInlineBase().gap     = VH(2);
card->getInlineBase().radius  = Px(8);

.card {
    padding: 3vh 2vw;
    gap: 2vh;
    radius: 8px;
}

docs.title: Centered modal
docs.text:
overlay->getInlineBase().itemsH = Align::Center;
overlay->getInlineBase().itemsV = Align::Center;
overlay->size(Percent(100), Percent(100));

.modal-overlay {
    width: 100%; height: 100%;
    items-h: center;
    items-v: center;
}

docs.title: Spacer that eats leftover space
docs.text:
sidebar->addChild(std::make_shared<Layout>()->cls("spacer-grow"));

.spacer-grow { grow: 1; }

docs.title: 13. Pitfalls
docs.text:
width: 100% on a child of an auto-sized parent. % resolves against the parent's width, which is being computed from its children — a circular dependency. ZenitUI breaks it by resolving the parent's auto size first (ignoring % children for that pass), then arranging. The result is usually "the child takes zero width". Give the parent an explicit width, or use grow: 1.

Forgetting to measure before arrange. arrange reads measuredSize from the previous measure. If you call arrange without a measure, sizes will be stale. runFrame does both in order; you only need to care if you're writing a custom loop.

gap on a Stack. Ignored. Stack has no main axis. Use padding on the container or margin on children.

justify has no effect when grow is set. justify only applies to leftover space. If a child has grow > 0, it will consume all the space, leaving nothing to justify. Remove grow if you want justify: center or space-between to work.

items-* vs align-*. items-h / items-v go on the container and are the default for all children. align-h / align-v go on the child and override the container's default. If you set them in both places, the child wins.

Absolute node with left: 0; right: 0; width: 100px. width wins — the node is 100px wide, positioned 0 from the left. right: 0 is ignored because width is not auto. Remove width if you want the node to stretch.

overflow: scroll without a fixed size. If the container has height: auto, its height grows to fit the content, so maxScroll is always zero and the scrollbar never appears. Give the container a bounded height (%, vh, or a parent with bounded height).

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
All built-in widgets live in namespace ZenitUI::UI. Every one of them is a subclass of Layout, so they all share the common API (see §2) and can be styled with .zstyle exactly like a plain Layout.

If you know a widget from CSS or another UI framework, most of the naming will feel familiar. Where it doesn't, this document explains the differences.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
Widget C++ class Factory helper ZMarkup tag Interactive Text / Label Text Label(text) Text, Label no Button Button Btn(text, cb) Button yes Panel Panel Pan() Panel no (blocks) Image ImageContainer — — no Toggle Toggle — Toggle yes Checkbox Checkbox — Checkbox yes Slider Slider — Slider yes Progress bar ProgressBar — ProgressBar no Text input TextInput — TextInput yes Scroll view ScrollView — ScrollView yes Dropdown Dropdown — Dropdown yes Canvas (render target) CanvasLayout — — — Modal Modal — — yes Tooltip Tooltip Tooltip::attach(...) — no Popup / Context menu Popup ContextMenu(items) — yes VStack / HStack (helpers) VStack(), HStack() VStack, HStack —

All widgets except helpers are created via their ::create(...) factory, not via std::make_shared. The factory calls onBuild() after construction, which is where composite widgets (Toggle, Dropdown, …) attach their internal children.

auto t = Toggle::create(true);      // ✅ right
auto t = std::make_shared<Toggle>(); // ❌ onBuild never runs

docs.title: 2. Common API
docs.text: Every widget inherits from Layout and therefore has:

docs.title: Fluent helpers
docs.text:
widget->cls("my-class");            // add a CSS class
widget->id("my-id");                // set the node id
widget->size(VW(10), VH(5));        // set width/height
widget->passThrough(true);          // click passes through to parent

docs.title: Inline style
docs.text:
widget->getInlineBase().background = Colors::Blue;
widget->getInlineBase().radius     = Px(8);

getInlineBase() returns a mutable Style&. Inline styles have the highest priority in the cascade (they beat any .zstyle rule).

docs.title: Tree
docs.text:
parent->addChild(widget);
widget->removeFromParent();
widget->children;                   // std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Layout>>

docs.title: State
docs.text:
widget->setEnabled(false);
widget->setInteractive(true);
widget->setFocusable(true);
widget->setKeyboardActivates(true);
widget->setChecked(true);           // for Toggle, Checkbox

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
All widgets support:

Callback Signature Fires when onClick void() Press + release on the same node. onPress void() Pointer down on the node. onRelease void() Pointer up on the node (regardless of press). onHoverEnter void() Pointer enters the node. onHoverExit void() Pointer leaves the node. onRightClick void() Right-click on the node.

See Events for bubbling and pointer-capture details.

docs.title: ZMarkup attributes
docs.text:
Every ZMarkup element accepts the same inline style attributes:

Button "OK" width="100px" height="40px" background="#FF0000" radius="8px"

For the full attribute list, see ZStyle §"Inline attributes".

docs.title: 3. Text / Label
docs.text: Plain text with wrapping, alignment, and font selection.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto t = Label("Hello, world!");
t->cls("normal-text");

auto wrapped = Label("A long paragraph that will wrap on multiple lines.");
wrapped->setWrap(true);
wrapped->size(Percent(100), Auto());

auto rich = Text::create("Replaced later");
rich->setText("New content");
rich->setFont(assets.getFont("mont"));

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Text "Hello, world"
Label.normal-text "Hello, world"
Text wrap "A long paragraph that will wrap..."

In ZMarkup, the string literal after the tag is the text content. wrap can be a bare flag (defaults to true) or wrap=false / wrap=true.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Description setText(std::string) Replace the text. setFont(FontHandle) Override the resolved font. setWrap(bool) Enable / disable wrapping. getWrap() Query the current setting.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Text {
    color: #FFFFFF;
    font-size: 3vh;
    letter-spacing: 2px;
    font: calibri;
    text-align: center;   /* start | center | end */
}

Text is not interactive. It has no pseudo-states.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Intrinsic size is the measured text box. With wrap, it depends on the available width — the parent must supply a bounded width, otherwise the text will never wrap.
  • text-align only affects the horizontal position of each line inside the node's rect. To center the node itself, use the parent's items-h: center.

docs.title: 4. Button
docs.text: A clickable box with a text child.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto b = Btn("Click me", []{
    std::printf("clicked\n");
});
b->cls("btn-primary");

// Full control — no auto text child
auto raw = Button::create([]{
    std::printf("clicked\n");
});
raw->addChild(Label("Custom")->cls("btn-text"));

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Button.btn-primary#go "Click me"

The ZMarkup factory uses Btn(text), so a Text child with class btn-text is added automatically.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Button itself only adds:

  • setInteractive(true)
  • setFocusable(true)
  • setKeyboardActivates(true)
  • default items-h: center, items-v: center
  • style tag "Button"

Everything else (background, padding, radius, hover effects) comes from .zstyle.

The callback is set through the constructor:

auto b = Button::create([]{ /* ... */ });

or, after building from ZMarkup, through the UINode handle:

ui.onClick("go", []{ /* ... */ });

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Button {
    radius: 8px;
    padding: 1.5vh 2vw;
    transition: background 0.25s ease-out, scale 0.12s ease-out;
}
Button:hover   { background: #3296FF; scale: 1.05; }
Button:pressed { background: #505050; scale: 0.95; }
Button:focus   { border-color: #FDF900; border-width: 2px; }
Button:disabled{ opacity: 0.4; }

.btn-primary { background: #0079F1; }
.btn-danger  { background: #BE2137; }

Button is the style tag. .btn-primary / .btn-danger are classes, typically applied together.

docs.title: 5. Panel
docs.text: A plain box. No content, no interaction, just a rectangle you can style.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto p = Pan();
p->cls("card");
p->addChild(Label("Inside the panel"));

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Panel.card {
    Text "Inside the panel"
}

Panel sets setInteractive(false) and setBlocksRaycast(true) — it won't receive clicks itself, but it will stop them from reaching things behind it.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Panel {
    background: #232328FF;
    radius: 8px;
}
.card {
    padding: 3vh;
    gap: 2vh;
    border-width: 1px;
    border-color: #3A3A40;
}

Panel is a Stack — children are overlaid, not flowed. For a flowed layout, use VStack / HStack or set display: vertical | horizontal in .zstyle (there's no display property in ZenitUI — see the note below).

Note: ZenitUI's LayoutType is set at construction, not through a style property. In .zstyle you cannot change Stack → Vertical. Use the right container from the start, or use VStack() / HStack() directly.

docs.title: 6. ImageContainer
docs.text: A node that draws a texture scaled to fill its rect.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto img = ImageContainer::create(assets.getTexture("bubble"));
img->size(Px(200), Px(200));

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Description setTexture(TextureHandle) Change the texture at runtime.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
The texture is stretched to fill the rect. tint colors the texture:

ImageContainer {
    tint: #FF0000FF;    /* multiplies the texture by red */
}

There is no ::part and no interaction.

docs.title: 7. Toggle
docs.text: An on/off switch. Renders a track (the node itself) and a knob (a child positioned by .zstyle).

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto t = Toggle::create(false);
t->onToggle = [](bool checked){
    std::printf("toggle: %d\n", checked);
};
t->setChecked(true);   // programmatic

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Toggle#t checked=true

ui.onToggle("t", [](bool v){ /* ... */ });

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method / field Description isChecked Public bool, the current state. onToggle std::function<void(bool)>, fires on user click. setChecked(bool) Programmatic state change (from Layout). getChecked() Current state (from Layout).

Toggle::create(state) sets the initial isChecked.

docs.title: Internal structure
docs.text:
Toggle::onBuild() creates one child:

  • a Layout with class toggle-knob.

Its geometry (position, size, radius) is set entirely through .zstyle. The .zstyle must set position: absolute on the knob and use Toggle:checked .toggle-knob to move it.

Toggle {
    width: 10vh;
    height: 5vh;
    radius: 50ph;
    background: #505050;
    transition: background 0.15s linear;
}
Toggle:checked { background: #00E430; }

Toggle .toggle-knob {
    position: absolute;
    width:  60ph;
    height: 60ph;
    top:    20ph;
    left:   20ph;
    radius: 50%;
    background: #FFFFFF;
    transition: left 0.28s ease-out-cubic;
}
Toggle:checked .toggle-knob {
    left: calc(100pw - 80ph);
}

The :checked state is a real CSS state — see Events §"State flags".

docs.title: 8. Checkbox
docs.text: A small box with a checkmark drawn directly (no child nodes).

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto c = Checkbox::create(false);
c->onToggle = [](bool v){ /* ... */ };

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text: Checkbox#c checked=true

docs.title: API
docs.text: Same as Toggle: isChecked, onToggle, setChecked.

docs.title: Intrinsic size
docs.text: font-size × 1.4. Override with width / height if you want a different size.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Checkbox draws its box and mark using the ::part mechanism:

Checkbox {
    background: #505050;   /* the box background */
    radius: 6px;
    transition: background 0.15s linear;
}
Checkbox:hover  { background: #606060; }
Checkbox:checked { background: #1574b0; }

Checkbox::box  { background: #1574b0; radius: 6px; }
Checkbox::mark { color: #FFFFFF; }
Checkbox:disabled::box  { background: #3A3A40; }
Checkbox:disabled::mark { color: #808080; }

::box is the outer rounded rect. ::mark is the small centered square that appears when checked. Both are painted by renderContent, not by children.

docs.title: 9. Slider
docs.text: A horizontal track with a draggable knob. Value is a float in [0, 1].

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto s = std::make_shared<Slider>(0.5f);
s->onValueChanged = [](float v){
    std::printf("value = %.2f\n", v);
};

Note: Slider is constructed directly (std::make_shared<Slider>(...)), not via ::create. There's no onBuild to run.

Actually, you can also use Slider::create(0.5f) if you prefer consistency — it works because TLayout generates both.

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Slider#s value=0.65 width="55%"

ui.onValueChanged("s", [](float v){ /* ... */ });

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method / field Description getValue() Current value in [0, 1]. onValueChanged std::function<void(float)>.

There is no setValue() — the value is only changed by user input (drag or keyboard). To set it programmatically, use getInlineBase()… no, that doesn't work either. If you need to set the value from code, keep a reference to the Slider and add a setter in your own code, or wrap it.

Note: the value is stored in a private field of Slider. There is currently no public API to set it programmatically after construction. The most common pattern is to build a small wrapper widget that owns both the Slider and your own state.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
• Drag: click anywhere on the track and drag. The knob follows the pointer, and pointer capture keeps events flowing even if the cursor leaves the node.
  • Keyboard: Left / Right move by 0.05. With Shift held, the step becomes 0.01.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Slider {
    color: #3296FF;   /* used by fill and knob if no override */
}
Slider::track { background: #1717cf; radius: 4px; }
Slider::fill  { color: #d6ff32; }
Slider::knob  { color: #d6ff32; }
Slider:hover::knob { animation: knobGlow 0.6s ease-in-out infinite; }
Slider:pressed::knob { animation: knobPop 0.2s ease-out; }
  • ::track is the background bar.
  • ::fill is the portion from the left to the current value.
  • ::knob is the circular handle.

All three are painted by renderContent. ::part rules support state pseudo-classes (:hover, :pressed, :checked, :focus, :disabled) — see ZStyle §"::part".

docs.title: 10. ProgressBar
docs.text: A non-interactive bar showing a value in [0, 1].

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto pb = std::make_shared<ProgressBar>(0.3f);
pb->setValue(0.7f);

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text: ProgressBar#pb value=0.3 width="55%"

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Description setValue(float) Change the value (clamped to [0, 1]). getValue() Current value.

docs.title: Intrinsic size
docs.text: 120 × max(16, font-size × 0.8).

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
ProgressBar {
    background: #2A2A32;
    color: #69ff32;   /* fill color */
    radius: 6px;
}
ProgressBar::track { background: #cc1c9d; }
ProgressBar::fill  { color: #69FF32; }

::track is the background bar. ::fill is the filled portion.

docs.title: 11. TextInput
docs.text: A single-line editable text field with a cursor, horizontal scrolling, and keyboard repeat.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto input = std::make_shared<TextInput>("Initial text");
input->onTextChanged = [](const std::string& s){
    std::printf("now: %s\n", s.c_str());
};
input->onSubmit = [](const std::string& s){
    std::printf("submitted: %s\n", s.c_str());
};

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
TextInput#name value="Player1" width="55%"

ui.onClick("name", ...);   // not needed — click focuses automatically

The value attribute sets the initial text.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method / field Description setText(std::string) Replace the content. getText() Current content. clear() Empty the input. setFont(FontHandle) Override the resolved font. onTextChanged std::function<void(const std::string&)>, fires on any edit. onSubmit std::function<void(const std::string&)>, fires on Enter.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
• Click → focuses the node.
  • Typing → inserts characters at the cursor. Only printable ASCII (0x20–0x7E) is accepted by default.
  • Backspace / Delete — delete around the cursor, with key repeat.
  • Left / Right — move the cursor, with key repeat.
  • Home / End — jump to start / end.
  • Enter — fires onSubmit, then releases focus.
  • Escape — releases focus without submitting.

Key repeat uses a 0.40s initial delay and 0.04s interval.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
TextInput {
    background: #1A1A20;
    color: #FFFFFF;
    radius: 6px;
    padding: 1.2vh 1.5vw;
    border-color: #505060;
    border-width: 2px;
    font-size: 3vh;
    transition: border-color 0.2s ease-out;
}
TextInput:focus { border-color: #FDF900; }

TextInput::cursor {
    color: #FF6600;
    border-width: 3px;
}
TextInput:hover::cursor {
    color: #FDF900;
    border-width: 10px;
}

::cursor is the blinking caret. Its border-width becomes the caret thickness; its color becomes the caret color. Blink period is 1s (half-visible, half-hidden).

docs.title: 12. ScrollView
docs.text: A Layout with overflow: scroll on both axes by default. Its actual behavior (clip, scrollbar, inertia, wheel) lives in Layout itself; the ScrollView class is just a convenience.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto sv = ScrollView::create(LayoutType::Vertical);
sv->addChild(Label("..."));
sv->addChild(Label("..."));
// many more children...

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
ScrollView#sv {
    Text "..."
    Text "..."
    // ...
}

docs.title: API
docs.text:
ScrollView adds no new methods beyond Layout. All scroll APIs are on Layout:

Method Description scrollTo(x, y) Absolute scroll position. scrollToTop() / scrollToBottom() Vertical. scrollToLeft() / scrollToRight() Horizontal. getScrollX() / getScrollY() Current offset. getMaxScrollX() / getMaxScrollY() Maximum offset. isScrollContainer() True if overflow is not visible on either axis.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
ScrollView {
    overflow: scroll;
    background: #1A1A20;
    radius: 8px;
    border-color: #505060;
    border-width: 2px;
    padding: 8px;
}

Set overflow-x: hidden / overflow-y: auto to disable one axis or make it appear only when needed. See Layout §8 Overflow.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The container's intrinsic size is {0, 0} — you must give it an explicit size (or a grow / shrink context) so it can actually scroll. A ScrollView with height: auto will never need to scroll.
  • Children with position: absolute inside a ScrollView are not scrolled (they're removed from flow before the scroll offset is applied). Use a normal child if you want it to move with the content.

docs.title: 13. Dropdown
docs.text: A button that opens a scrollable list of options. The list is a portal — it renders above everything else, ignoring clipping and z-index of the surrounding tree.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto dd = Dropdown::create(
    std::vector<std::string>{"Easy", "Normal", "Hard"},
    1   // default selection index
);

dd->onChange = [](int idx, const std::string& name){
    std::printf("picked %d: %s\n", idx, name.c_str());
};

docs.title: ZMarkup
docs.text:
Dropdown#diff options="Facile,Normale,Difficile"

ui.find<Dropdown>("diff")->onChange = [](int i, const std::string& n){ /* ... */ };

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method / field Description getSelected() Current index. setSelected(int) Programmatically change selection. Fires onChange. getOpen() / setOpen(bool) Control the open state. onChange std::function<void(int, const std::string&)>.

docs.title: Internal structure
docs.text:
Dropdown::onBuild() creates:

  1. A Button with class dropdown-trigger — the closed-state face.
  2. A ScrollView with position: absolute and setPortal(true) — the list of options. Each option is a Label with padding and an onClick that sets the selection.

The list's position is computed every frame in arrange():

  • Default: below the trigger, offset by 4px.
  • If there isn't enough space below, it flips above.
  • If it doesn't fit on either side, it's shrunk to the largest available space.

Closing on outside click is handled in onUpdate. Clicking anywhere that isn't the trigger or the list closes the dropdown.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
The trigger's visual properties live in inlineDefaults, so a .zstyle rule can override them freely:

.dropdown-trigger {
    height: 48px;                       /* default: 3vh */
    background: #232328;
    radius: 6px;
    padding: 8px 14px;
    border-width: 1px;
    border-color: #505060;
    font-size: 16px;
}
.dropdown-trigger .btn-text {
    font-size: 16px;
}

Dropdown { background: #232328; }   /* affects the trigger face */

Only width: 100% is baked into the trigger's inlineBase — it's what makes the trigger fill its logical parent. To constrain the dropdown's overall width, wrap it in a fixed-size container:

auto wrapper = std::make_shared<Layout>(LayoutType::Stack);
wrapper->size(Px(180), Auto());
wrapper->addChild(dropdown);
parent->addChild(wrapper);

This is the recommended pattern when placing a dropdown inside an HStack or any other container that would otherwise let the trigger stretch to the full row width.

Individual options inherit whatever styling you apply to Label inside the list. The list itself (ScrollView) can be targeted via Dropdown ScrollView { ... }.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The list is a portal, so it is not clipped by ancestor overflow: hidden. This is the entire reason portals exist.
  • setOpen(false) when the dropdown is disabled — the implementation closes it automatically in onEnabledChanged.
  • The trigger's height, background, radius, border-*, items-h, and items-v are all overridable via .zstyle. Only width: 100% is fixed.
  • If the trigger's text is invisible, check the trigger's padding against its height. If padding-top + padding-bottom is larger than the trigger's content box, the text gets clipped to zero height.

docs.title: 14. Canvas (render target)
docs.text: A CanvasLayout renders its subtree into an offscreen render target, then draws that target as a texture. Useful for effects that need to be applied to a subtree as a whole, or for caching complex subtrees.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto canvas = std::make_shared<CanvasLayout>();
canvas->size(Px(400), Px(300));
canvas->addChild(someHeavySubtree);

// Optional: apply a shader to the whole canvas
canvas->setShader(assets.getEffect("hueShift"));

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The render target is recreated whenever the node's rect size changes.
  • The target is destroyed in the destructor.
  • supports(Feature::Effects) is required for the shader to be applied; the Raylib backend supports it.
  • CanvasLayout is Stack type.

There is no ZMarkup tag for Canvas by default. You can register one yourself via ZMarkup::Registry::reg("Canvas", ...).

docs.title: 15. Modal
docs.text: A full-screen overlay with a centered content panel and an intro animation.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
auto modal = Modal::create();
modal->children[0]->addChild(Label("Are you sure?"));
modal->addChild(...) → don't. Use the content VStack inside.

// Actually: children[0] is the content VStack with class "modal-content"
auto content = modal->children[0];
content->addChild(Label("Are you sure?"));
content->addChild(Btn("OK", [modal]{ modal->hide(); }));

parent->addChild(modal);
modal->show();

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Description show() Set opacity to 1 and play the intro animation. hide() Set opacity to 0 and play the intro in reverse.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Modal::onBuild() creates:

  • A full-screen Stack with tag "Modal", black background at 0.6 opacity, setFocusScope(true).
  • One child: a VStack with class modal-content. This is where you put your content.

The intro animation ("Intro") translates the content from VH(100) (bottom) to 0 using ease-out-back.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Modal { background: #000000CC; }
.modal-content {
    width: 60vw;
    padding: 4vh;
    gap: 2vh;
    background: #1E1E24;
    radius: 12px;
}

Modal is a focus scope — pressing Tab inside it cycles through its focusable descendants only, not the whole tree. See Events §"Focus scopes".

docs.title: 16. Tooltip
docs.text: A small floating box shown when hovering its owner, after a delay.

docs.title: C++ — attach to an owner
docs.text:
auto btn = Btn("Save", []{});
Tooltip::attach(btn, "Save your changes", 0.4f);

attach(owner, text, showDelay):

  1. Creates the tooltip.
  2. Sets owner as its anchor.
  3. Hooks into owner->onHoverEnter / onHoverExit to start / stop the show timer.
  4. Adds the tooltip as a child of owner (for lifetime) but renders it as a portal.

docs.title: Manual control
docs.text:
auto tip = Tooltip::create("Hello");
tip->setAnchor(someNode);
tip->setShowDelay(0.5f);
someNode->addChild(tip);

tip->show();   // starts the delay timer
tip->hide();   // hides immediately

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Description attach(owner, text, delay) Static. Convenience. setAnchor(Layout*) Node the tooltip is positioned relative to. setShowDelay(float) Seconds before the tooltip appears. show() / hide() Manual control.

docs.title: Positioning
docs.text: The tooltip is centered above its anchor, offset by 6px vertically. If the anchor has not been measured yet, the tooltip is not positioned.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Tooltip {
    background: #000000E6;
    color: #FFFFFF;
    padding: 0.6vh 0.8vw;
    radius: 4px;
    border-color: #606070;
    border-width: 1px;
    transition: opacity 0.2s ease-out;
}

Tooltips are Panel subclasses with setPortal(true) and setBlocksRaycast(false). They don't capture input.

docs.title: 17. Popup / ContextMenu
docs.text: A floating panel that can be opened below, above, or at an arbitrary screen position. Used for context menus, dropdown menus, and tooltips that need more interactivity than Tooltip.

docs.title: C++ — as a menu
docs.text:
auto menu = ContextMenu({
    { "Copy",  []{ /* ... */ } },
    { "Paste", []{ /* ... */ } },
    { "Delete",[]{ /* ... */ } },
});

someNode->addChild(menu);   // lifetime
someNode->onClick      = [menu, someNode]{ menu->openBelow(someNode); };
